moduleTitle: SQE1 · Legal System and Legal Services
title: The Legal Services Act 2007: regulatory objectives and reserved legal activities
subtitle: The eight regulatory objectives, the six reserved legal activities, and why unauthorised practice is a criminal offence
objectives: List the eight regulatory objectives set out in the Legal Services Act 2007 and explain the purpose they collectively serve
Identify the six reserved legal activities and explain why carrying one out without authorisation is a criminal offence
Apply the reserved-activities framework to a fact pattern to determine whether a described activity requires authorisation

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the eight regulatory objectives that approved regulators and the Legal Services Board must promote

leadingAuthorities.citation: Legal Services Act 2007, s 12 and Sch 2
leadingAuthorities.role: Defines the six reserved legal activities
Sets the entitlement test for lawfully carrying on a reserved legal activity
Makes carrying on a reserved legal activity without entitlement a criminal offence

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: It's easy to memorise 'six reserved activities' as a list. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the list — this lesson is about spotting when an everyday task is quietly one of them.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on short scenarios: expect to identify whether a described activity is reserved, not to recite the list.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Parts 1 and 2 and take your time over the eight objectives and the six reserved activities — later parts assume you can name both sets without prompting.

overview.hook: A man sets up a kitchen-table business drafting wills for a fee, with no qualification and no regulator. Is that a crime? For one narrow class of legal work, framed in exactly those terms, the answer under the Legal Services Act 2007 can genuinely be yes — and the Act exists precisely to draw that line, and to say why it is drawn there.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The list of reserved legal activities and the eight regulatory objectives are fixed points in the current statutory scheme, but the regulatory landscape around them (approved regulator mergers, CILEX Regulation's evolving remit, and periodic government review of legal services regulation) has been subject to ongoing consultation — treat the institutional detail, though not the core statutory list, as an area to keep current.

parts.heading: Why the Act exists: regulating for a purpose, not for its own sake
parts.voice: argumentative — states the rationale before the list
body: The Legal Services Act 2007 was the product of a review that concluded legal services regulation had grown up piecemeal, profession by profession, with no shared sense of what regulation was actually for. The Act's answer was to require every approved regulator, and the Legal Services Board overseeing them, to act in a way that promotes a common set of regulatory objectives, set out in s 1.

This matters more than it sounds. The objectives are not decorative preamble — they are the yardstick against which regulatory decisions can be tested and, where a regulator strays from them, challenged. A rule a regulator makes that cannot be justified by reference to the objectives is a rule on shaky ground.

There are eight objectives, and they deliberately pull in more than one direction at once — protecting consumers is not the same project as protecting competition, and a mature regulatory system has to hold both in view rather than optimise for either alone.

components.definition: One of eight statutory aims, set out in Legal Services Act 2007, s 1, that the Legal Services Board and every approved regulator must act in a way that is compatible with, and must seek to promote, in regulating legal services.

interaction.prompt: Under the Legal Services Act 2007, who must act compatibly with, and seek to promote, the regulatory objectives?
options: Only the Legal Services Board
The Legal Services Board and every approved regulator
Only the SRA
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the duty runs across the whole regulatory architecture, not just the oversight body at the top.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again — the duty is not confined to the Legal Services Board alone. Every approved regulator (the SRA, the Bar Standards Board, CILEX Regulation, and others) is bound by it too.

parts.heading: The eight objectives
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Learn these as a set, because SQE1 questions often test whether you can spot which objective a given regulatory decision is serving, rather than asking you to recite the list cold.

Several of the eight sit in obvious tension, and that tension is the point: a regulator promoting access to justice by lowering barriers to entry has to weigh that against promoting a strong, effective and independent profession, or protecting consumer interests against under-qualified providers.

components.label: The eight regulatory objectives (Legal Services Act 2007, s 1)
points: Protecting and promoting the public interest
Supporting the constitutional principle of the rule of law
Protecting and promoting the interests of consumers
Promoting competition in the provision of legal services
Encouraging an independent, strong, diverse and effective legal profession
Increasing public understanding of the citizen's legal rights and duties
Promoting and maintaining adherence to the professional principles (independence, integrity, client interests, proper standards of work, and duties to the court)

interaction.prompt: Tap the phrase in this regulatory statement that most clearly engages the 'access to justice' objective, as opposed to the others listed.
interaction.scenarioText: The Legal Services Board notes that new online guidance for litigants in person has reduced the proportion of unrepresented parties who abandon a claim before a hearing due to confusion about procedure.
tappableSpans: online guidance for litigants in person
reduced the proportion of unrepresented parties
abandon a claim before a hearing
interaction.correctSpan: reduced the proportion of unrepresented parties
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the access-to-justice outcome directly: fewer people are shut out of pursuing a claim they are otherwise entitled to bring.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the outcome, not the mechanism or the problem it addresses. Access to justice is about who actually gets to pursue their claim, not the guidance itself or the underlying confusion.

parts.heading: Reserved legal activities: the narrow list that requires authorisation
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the list through the logic of why it exists
body: Most legal work is not regulated by title at all. Anyone can call themselves a 'legal consultant' and give general legal advice — that is not, in itself, a reserved activity. What the Act reserves is a short, specific list of activities considered to carry enough risk to the public or to the administration of justice that carrying them out without authorisation is a criminal offence.

Section 12 and Schedule 2 of the Act set out six reserved legal activities: the exercise of a right of audience; the conduct of litigation; reserved instrument activities (broadly, preparing documents relating to real or personal estate transactions, such as transfers of land, for money or money's worth); probate activities; notarial activities; and the administration of oaths.

Notice what is not on the list: general legal advice, drafting a contract for a friend, or representing yourself. The reserved list is deliberately narrow — it targets specific activities, not 'legal work' as a broad category.

components.label: The six reserved legal activities (LSA 2007, s 12 and Sch 2)
points: The exercise of a right of audience
Reserved instrument activities (property transaction documents for money or money's worth)

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that identifies the general legal-advice work that is NOT a reserved activity.
interaction.passage: The six reserved legal activities are a narrow, specific list — the exercise of a right of audience, the conduct of litigation, reserved instrument activities, probate activities, notarial activities, and the administration of oaths. General legal advice, by contrast, is not itself a reserved activity and may lawfully be given by an unqualified person, though giving bad advice may expose that person to other liability.
interaction.ratioSentence: General legal advice, by contrast, is not itself a reserved activity and may lawfully be given by an unqualified person, though giving bad advice may expose that person to other liability.

parts.heading: Why unauthorised practice is a crime, not just misconduct
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Here's a question worth sitting with: why does English law make it a criminal offence — not merely a regulatory breach, not merely something actionable in negligence — to conduct someone's litigation without authorisation, when it is perfectly lawful to give them wrong legal advice generally?

The Act's answer, embedded in ss 13 and 14, is that the six reserved activities are ones where the risk of unqualified practice is judged serious enough, and detection after the fact difficult enough, that the criminal law is used to deter the conduct before it happens, rather than relying on the client to sue afterwards. Section 13 sets the entitlement test — authorisation by a relevant approved regulator, or an exemption; s 14 then makes it an offence to carry on a reserved activity without meeting that test.

This is why the list in Part 3 has to be learned precisely rather than approximately. Someone giving confident but wrong general legal advice on a contract has, at most, exposed themselves to a civil claim. Someone conducting litigation on a client's behalf without authorisation has committed a criminal offence, however competently they did it and however good the outcome for the client.

components.text: It is an offence for a person to carry on an activity ('the relevant activity') which is a reserved legal activity unless that person is entitled to carry on that activity.
elements: The activity carried on must be a reserved legal activity
The person carrying it on must lack entitlement under s 13
No requirement that the person acted dishonestly, incompetently, or caused any loss

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a person can commit the s 14 offence even where they carried out the reserved activity competently and the client suffered no loss?
sliderLabels: Not an offence without loss or incompetence
Still an offence regardless of competence or loss
interaction.correctPosition: Still an offence regardless of competence or loss
interaction.explanation: Section 14 turns on entitlement, not on the quality of the work done or whether the client was harmed. Competent, well-intentioned unauthorised practice of a reserved activity is still the offence — the harm the section targets is the absence of authorisation itself.

parts.heading: Applying the framework: is this activity reserved?
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: SQE1 questions in this area typically describe an activity and ask whether it is reserved, or whether a particular person may lawfully carry it out. The trap is treating anything that 'sounds legal' as reserved, when the list in s 12 and Sch 2 is narrow and specific.

Drafting a witness statement, for example, is not itself a reserved activity, even though it is closely tied to litigation — conduct of litigation covers issuing and progressing proceedings, not every document connected with a case. Similarly, administering an oath is reserved, but simply witnessing a signature generally is not, unless it specifically involves administering an oath or statutory declaration.

The reliable method: identify the precise activity described, check it against the six-item list exactly (not against a vague sense of 'legal-sounding'), and only then decide whether authorisation is required.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that any activity closely connected with litigation or property — drafting a witness statement, giving advice on a lease, negotiating a settlement — must itself be a reserved activity.
components.whyItsWrong: The reserved list is activity-specific and narrow. Conduct of litigation, for instance, covers the formal issuing, commencing and prosecuting of proceedings — not every task that touches litigation, such as advising a client informally or drafting a supporting document. Overinclusion is the most common error in this area.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario describes a reserved legal activity requiring authorisation?
interaction.scenarioA: An unqualified adviser drafts a detailed letter setting out a client's legal position on a contract dispute, for a fee.
interaction.scenarioB: An unqualified adviser issues and files a claim form at court on the client's behalf, in order to formally commence proceedings.
interaction.explanation: Issuing and filing a claim form to commence proceedings falls within the conduct of litigation, a reserved legal activity. Drafting an advisory letter, however detailed, is general legal advice and not itself reserved.

testPool.prompt: How many regulatory objectives are set out in Legal Services Act 2007, s 1?
options: Six
Seven
Eight
Ten
testPool.explanation: Section 1 sets out eight regulatory objectives, ranging from protecting the public interest to promoting adherence to the professional principles.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the six reserved legal activities under Legal Services Act 2007, Sch 2?
options: The conduct of litigation
Reserved instrument activities
Giving general legal advice on a client's rights
The administration of oaths
testPool.trapExplanation: General legal advice is exactly the kind of everyday 'legal-sounding' work students assume must be reserved. It is not on the list — the reserved activities are a narrow, specific set, and general advice-giving is not among them.
testPool.explanation: General legal advice is not a reserved legal activity and may lawfully be given by an unqualified person. The six reserved activities are rights of audience, conduct of litigation, reserved instrument activities, probate activities, notarial activities, and administration of oaths.

testPool.prompt: What does Legal Services Act 2007, s 14 provide in relation to a person who carries out a reserved legal activity without entitlement?
options: They may face a regulatory fine only, imposed by the Legal Services Board
They commit a criminal offence
They are liable only in negligence to the client
Nothing, provided the client consented
testPool.explanation: Section 14 makes carrying on a reserved legal activity without the entitlement required by s 13 a criminal offence, regardless of client consent or the standard of work done.

testPool.prompt: An unqualified individual, for a fee, prepares and signs a transfer document conveying a client's house to a buyer for money. Which reserved legal activity, if any, has most likely been carried out?
options: Probate activities
Reserved instrument activities
The conduct of litigation
No reserved activity — property documents are never reserved
testPool.explanation: Preparing an instrument relating to a real estate transaction for money or money's worth falls within reserved instrument activities, one of the six reserved legal activities under Sch 2.

testPool.prompt: Which regulatory objective specifically addresses the constitutional role of the legal system, rather than the quality or accessibility of legal services?
options: Improving access to justice
Supporting the constitutional principle of the rule of law
Promoting competition in the provision of legal services
Increasing public understanding of legal rights and duties
testPool.explanation: Supporting the constitutional principle of the rule of law is a distinct objective from the service-quality and access-focused objectives, and reflects the Act's recognition that legal services regulation sits within a wider constitutional setting.

testPool.prompt: A litigant in person drafts and files their own claim form at court, without instructing anyone else to act for them. Have they committed the s 14 offence?
options: Yes, because filing a claim form is conduct of litigation
No, because a person is always entitled to conduct their own litigation in person
Yes, unless they first obtain permission from the court
No, but only if the claim is worth less than the small claims limit
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes over-apply the reserved-activities list, forgetting that the framework governs unauthorised persons acting on behalf of others, not a party conducting their own case. Acting for yourself has never required authorisation.
testPool.explanation: The reserved-activities scheme governs a person carrying out reserved work for someone else without authorisation. Conducting one's own litigation in person has never required authorisation and is not caught by s 14.

testPool.prompt: Which combination of provisions together establish that unauthorised exercise of a reserved legal activity is unlawful and criminal?
options: Sections 1 and 12 alone
Sections 13 and 14 together
Schedule 2 alone
Section 1 alone
testPool.explanation: Section 13 sets the entitlement test (authorisation by an approved regulator, or exemption); s 14 then criminalises carrying on a reserved activity without meeting that test. The two provisions work together.

testPool.prompt: A person who is not a solicitor, barrister or other authorised person is asked by a friend to administer an oath in connection with a statutory declaration. What is the position?
options: This is freely permitted, as administering an oath is not reserved
This is a reserved legal activity, and carrying it out without authorisation is a criminal offence
This is only reserved if a fee is charged
This is only reserved in criminal proceedings
testPool.explanation: Administration of oaths is one of the six reserved legal activities under Sch 2, so carrying it out without authorisation by a relevant approved regulator is a criminal offence under s 14.

testPool.prompt: Why do the eight regulatory objectives sometimes point in different directions for a given regulatory decision?
options: Because the Act contains a drafting error that will eventually be corrected
Because objectives such as access to justice, competition, and a strong profession reflect genuinely different interests that a mature regulatory system must balance
Because only one objective actually applies at any given time
Because the objectives apply only to the Legal Services Board, never to individual regulators
testPool.explanation: The objectives are deliberately broad and can conflict — for example, wider access via lower entry barriers can sit in tension with maintaining a strong, effective profession. Balancing them, not mechanically satisfying each, is the regulatory task.

testPool.prompt: A student lists 'promoting the interests of shareholders in law firms' as one of the eight regulatory objectives. Is this correct?
options: Yes, this is objective five
No — the objectives include promoting consumer interests and competition, but not shareholder interests specifically
Yes, but only for alternative business structures
No, because the Act has no objective relating to competition or business interests at all
testPool.trapExplanation: The objectives do include market-facing aims (competition, a strong profession) but shareholder interests as such are not among the eight — students sometimes invent a plausible-sounding ninth objective under exam pressure.
testPool.explanation: The eight objectives cover the public interest, the rule of law, access to justice, consumer interests, competition, a strong and effective profession, public understanding, and the professional principles — not shareholder interests, which is not a recognised objective.

testPool.prompt: A retired solicitor, whose practising certificate has lapsed, agrees to represent a neighbour's interests in County Court proceedings and stands up to argue the case. What is the most accurate description of the position?
options: This is lawful because she was once a qualified solicitor
This is likely the s 14 offence, because she is exercising a right of audience without current entitlement
This is lawful provided the neighbour does not pay her
This is lawful because County Court proceedings are excluded from the reserved-activities scheme
testPool.explanation: Entitlement under s 13 depends on current authorisation, not past qualification. With a lapsed practising certificate, she is not currently authorised, so exercising a right of audience on the neighbour's behalf is likely to be the s 14 offence, payment or not.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes probate activities as a reserved legal activity?
options: Any advice on inheritance tax planning
Applying for a grant of probate or letters of administration and associated preparation of papers, for or in expectation of a fee
Simply being named as an executor in a will
Any discussion of a deceased person's estate with the family
testPool.explanation: Probate activities as a reserved legal activity centre on preparing papers for, and applying for, a grant of probate or letters of administration for or in expectation of a fee — not general inheritance advice or informal family discussion.

testPool.prompt: A management consultant, unqualified in law, negotiates the commercial terms of a settlement between two businesses but takes no steps to issue, file or progress any court proceedings. Has she carried out a reserved legal activity?
options: Yes, because any involvement in a dispute is conduct of litigation
No, because conduct of litigation requires the formal issuing, commencing or progressing of proceedings, which did not occur here
Yes, because she charged a fee for her services
No, but only because the parties later settled
testPool.trapExplanation: Fee-charging and general dispute involvement are easy to mistake for the trigger, but neither is the test. Conduct of litigation is defined by formal procedural steps in relation to court proceedings, not by dispute-related work generally.
testPool.explanation: Conduct of litigation covers formal steps such as issuing, commencing and prosecuting proceedings. Purely commercial negotiation, however fee-earning and dispute-related, does not by itself amount to this reserved activity.

testPool.prompt: Which body's duty to act compatibly with, and promote, the regulatory objectives sits at the top of the regulatory structure created by the Act?
options: The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal
The Legal Services Board
The Legal Ombudsman
The Law Society
testPool.explanation: The Legal Services Board is the oversight body at the top of the structure created by the Act, itself bound by the s 1 objectives and responsible for overseeing the approved regulators that are also bound by them.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is overinclusion — assuming that anything 'legal-sounding' or fee-earning must be a reserved activity. The list in s 12 and Sch 2 is short and specific; check the precise activity against it rather than against a general sense of legal work.
